query: The Co-free FeNiCrMn system was selected to reduce cost while retaining the mechanical performance of equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi; prior work reported comparable or better mechanical properties after excluding Co. Research on FeNiCrMn has mainly addressed corrosion, while studies of related high- and medium-entropy alloys examined dynamic responses under tension or compression, different temperatures and strain rates, compositional changes, and the presence of cracks or voids. Those studies established that dynamic properties are sensitive to loading regime and material condition, but their different chemistries and defect states do not identify what governs FeNiCrMn. Under the constraints of retaining the Co-free composition and its strength–ductility balance, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis explains the dynamic behavior of solidified FeNiCrMn across temperature and strain-rate regimes? Define a controlled study capable of testing the hypothesis, its applicable boundaries, the prior findings that support it, and a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In the as‐cast, solid‐solution Co‐free FeNiCrMn alloy, the dynamic mechanical response across a broad temperature and strain‐rate range is primarily governed by thermally activated dislocation slip that is modulated by local lattice distortions arising from inherent chemical inhomogeneity. At lower temperatures and/or slow strain rates, strong dislocation pinning by lattice distortions elevates the yield strength but suppresses work hardening and ductility, whereas at intermediate temperatures and high strain rates, enhanced thermal activation leads to increased dislocation mobility and interactions, promoting greater work hardening and ductility while maintaining an optimal strength–ductility balance.
generation.material_initial_state: As-cast, single-phase solid solution featuring nanoscale lattice distortions due to multi-principal element chemical inhomogeneity.
generation.intervention: Uniaxial tensile and compressive deformation experiments conducted on cast FeNiCrMn specimens over a range of temperatures (from cryogenic to high temperatures) and strain rates (from quasi-static to dynamic).
generation.conditions: Testing must span low, intermediate, and high temperature regimes as well as slow to dynamic strain-rate conditions, ensuring that the material remains in a metastable single-phase state without secondary precipitate formation.
generation.structural_mediator: Local lattice distortions and the distribution of dislocation pinning sites resulting from chemical inhomogeneity.
generation.mechanism: Thermal activation modulates the overcoming of dislocation pinning sites caused by lattice distortions. At low temperatures, insufficient thermal energy leads to strong pinning and limited dislocation glide, increasing yield strength but reducing ductility. Conversely, at higher temperatures and under rapid loading, increased dislocation mobility and interactions (including dynamic recovery and dislocation entanglement) contribute to enhanced work hardening and a favorable strength–ductility balance.
generation.predicted_outcome: Under quasi-static, room-temperature conditions, the alloy exhibits moderate yield strength with balanced ductility. At lower temperatures or very low strain rates, yield strength increases with a reduced ductility due to limited dislocation motion, while at elevated temperatures and higher strain rates, an increase in work hardening and ductility is observed as thermally-assisted dislocation motion becomes dominant. Deviations from this trend (e.g., absence of improved plasticity at higher strain rates) would undermine the hypothesis.
generation.baseline: Mechanical properties observed at room temperature and quasi-static strain rates serve as the reference state.
generation.boundary: This mechanistic explanation is limited to the as-cast, single-phase FeNiCrMn alloy; it may not apply if the processing introduces secondary phases, coarse precipitates, or significant microstructural heterogeneity.
generation.uncertainty: The quantitative contributions of thermal activation and dislocation pinning, including activation energies and critical strain-rate thresholds, remain to be calibrated by detailed experimentation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare as-cast FeNiCrMn alloy specimens and perform in situ uniaxial tensile and compressive tests under controlled environmental conditions. Vary the test temperature (e.g., cryogenic, room temperature, and elevated temperature) and strain rate (from quasi-static to high dynamic rates). Simultaneously, utilize high-resolution digital image correlation (DIC) and/or in situ transmission electron microscopy (TEM) to monitor dislocation activity, lattice distortions, and the evolution of the microstructure.
measurements: Yield strength and flow stress at different temperatures and strain rates
Work hardening rate and tensile ductility
Dislocation density and mobility via in situ TEM or DIC strain mapping
Activation of microstructural mechanisms (e.g., evidence of dynamic recovery or dislocation pinning)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the mechanical property trends (yield strength, work hardening rate, and ductility) do not correlate with the predicted shifts in dislocation behavior (i.e., if no significant modulation in dislocation activity due to thermal activation and lattice distortion is observed across the tested temperature and strain rate regimes), or if alternative mechanisms (such as phase transformations or precipitation) are found to be dominant, the hypothesis is falsified.

Evaluation of Equiatomic CrMnFeCoNiCu System and Subsequent Derivation of a Non-Equiatomic MnFeCoNiCu Alloy

Abstract: AbstractInvestigation into non-equiatomic high-entropy alloys has grown in recent years due to questions about the role of entropy stabilization in forming single-phase solid solutions. Non-equiatomic alloys have been shown to retain the outstanding mechanical properties exhibited by their equiatomic counterparts and even improve electrical, thermal, and magnetic properties, albeit with relaxed composition bounds. However, much remains to understand the processing–structure–property relationships in all classes of so-called high-entropy alloys (HEAs). Here, we are motivated by the natural phenomena of crystal growth and equilibrium conditions to introduce a method of HEA development where controlled processing conditions determine the most probable and stable composition. This is demonstrated by cooling an equiatomic CrMnFeCoNiCu alloy from the melt steadily over 3 days (cooling rate ~4 °C/h). Combining Machine Learning and Molecular Dynamics to Predict Mechanical Properties and Microstructural Evolution of FeNiCrCoCu High-Entropy Alloys

Abstract: AbstractCompared with traditional alloys, high-entropy alloys have better mechanical properties and corrosion resistance. However, their mechanical properties and microstructural evolution behavior are unclear due to their complex composition. Machine learning has powerful data processing and analysis capabilities, that provides technical advantages for in-depth study of the mechanical properties of high-entropy alloys. Thus, we combined machine learning and molecular dynamics to predict the mechanical properties of FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy alloys. The optimal multiple linear regression machine learning algorithm predicts that the optimal composition is Fe33Ni32Cr11Co11Cu13 high-entropy alloy, with a tensile strength of 28.25 GPa. Furthermore, molecular dynamics is used to verify the predicted mechanical properties of high-entropy alloys, and it is found that the error between the tensile strength predicted by machine learning and the tensile strength obtained by molecular dynamics simulation is within 0.5%. High-Temperature Mechanical Properties of NbTaHfTiZrV0.5 Refractory High-Entropy Alloys

Abstract: AbstractThe NbTaHfTiZrV0.5 is a refractory multi-principal-element alloy with high strength and good ductility at room temperature. It is important for possible high-temperature applications to investigate the deformation mechanism of the NbTaHfTiZrV0.5 alloy at different temperatures using tensile tests. In this investigation, the tensile tests were conducted at room temperature to 1273 K on sheet materials fabricated by cold rolling combined with annealing treatments. At 473 K, the NbTaHfTiZrV0.5 alloy exhibited a high tensile ductility (12%). At a testing temperature range of 673~873 K, the ductility was reduced, but the yield strength remained above 800 MPa, which is rare in most other alloys. The TEM investigations revealed that a dislocation slip controlled the plastic deformation, and the degree of deformation was closely related to the dislocation density. The true stress–strain curves of the alloy under different deformation conditions were obtained by tensile deformation at different deformation temperatures (673~873 K) and strain rates (0.001~0.0005 s−1). Effect of scanning speeds on mechanical properties of CoCrNi medium entropy alloy prepared by laser additive manufacturing

Abstract: Medium entropy alloy (MEA) is a hot spot in the field of material research in recent years. At present, the most widely used processing method of MEAs is “casting-rolling-heat treatment”, and the preparation of CoCrNi MEA by laser additive manufacturing (LAM) is still in primary stage. In this study, CoCrNi MEAs were fabricated with different scanning speeds by laser additive manufacturing, and the influence of scanning speed on its mechanical properties was investigated. The results show that higher scanning speed can significantly improve the mechanical properties of CoCrNi MEA. Compared with the low-speed laser additive manufacturing (LSLAM) MEA, the tensile strength of high-speed laser additive manufacturing (HSLAM) MEA is increased by 5.6 % and the fracture strain is increased by 60 %, which is mainly due to the entanglement of 1/6<112> and 1/2<110> dislocations and the defect structure at the grain boundary. LAM is a promising technology that can promote the development and application of MEAs in industry.

Elastic strain-induced amorphization in high-entropy alloys

Abstract: AbstractElastic stability is the basis for understanding structural responses to external stimuli in crystalline solids, including melting, incipient plasticity and fracture. In this work, elastic stability is investigated in a series of high-entropy alloys (HEAs) using in situ mechanical tests and atomic-resolution characterization in transmission electron microscopy. Under tensile loading, the HEA lattices are observed to undergo a sudden loss of ordering as the elastic strain reached ∽ 10%. Such elastic strain-induced amorphization stands in intrinsic contrast to previously reported dislocation-mediated elastic instability and defect accumulation-mediated amorphization, introducing a form of elastic instability. Together with the first principle calculations and atomic-resolution chemical mapping, we identify that the elastic strain-induced amorphization is closely related to the depressed dislocation nucleation due to the local atomic environment inhomogeneity of HEAs.
